message.content: Read redu.md and deploy Calibre Web Automated on redu.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

attachment.content:
- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.
- aws-billing-and-cost-management: Analyze AWS costs, find savings, manage budgets, evaluate Savings Plans and Reserved Instances, right-size EC2/Lambda/RDS/EBS with Compute Optimizer, look up service pricing, query CUR with Athena, detect cost anomalies, scope costs to billing views, and monitor Free Tier usage. Triggers on: AWS bill, cost analysis, reduce spend, savings plan, reserved instance, right-size, budget alert, cost optimization, pricing, free tier, cost anomaly, CUR, cost audit, billing view, billing view ARN.
- aws-blocks: Guides building full-stack applications with AWS Blocks — an Infrastructure-from-Code framework. Applies when creating APIs, selecting Building Blocks (KVStore, DistributedTable, Database, AuthBasic, AuthCognito, Realtime, AsyncJob, FileBucket, etc.), running local development, or deploying AWS Blocks applications. Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Triggers when user mentions AWS Blocks; project has aws-blocks/ directory; code imports @aws-blocks packages.
- aws-cdk: Authors, deploys, and troubleshoots AWS infrastructure using CDK with TypeScript or Python. Covers best practices, stack architecture, and construct patterns. Always use when writing CDK constructs, bootstrapping environments, running cdk deploy/synth/diff, fixing CDK or CloudFormation errors, planning stack structure, importing existing resources, resolving drift, or refactoring stacks without resource replacement.
- aws-cloudformation: Author, validate, and troubleshoot AWS CloudFormation templates. Covers template authoring with secure defaults, pre-deployment validation (cfn-lint, cfn-guard, change sets), and root-cause diagnosis of failed stacks using CloudFormation events and CloudTrail correlation.
- aws-containers: Deploys and operates containerized workloads on ECS, Fargate, and ECR. Covers task definitions, Fargate services, ECR repository setup and lifecycle policies, ECS Exec debugging, service scaling, deployment strategies, load balancer integration, and logging configuration. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.
- aws-messaging-and-streaming: Guides use of AWS messaging and streaming services. Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.
- aws-sdk-js-v3-usage: AWS SDK for JavaScript v3 development patterns. Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.
- aws-sdk-swift-usage: AWS SDK for Swift development patterns. Use when writing Swift code that uses AWS services via aws-sdk-swift package.
- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Covers cold starts, CORS debugging, event source mappings, troubleshooting, concurrency, SnapStart, Powertools, function URLs, EventBridge Scheduler, Lambda layers, and production readiness. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." Does not apply to EC2, ECS/Fargate containers, or Amplify hosting.
- cso: Chief Security Officer mode. (gstack)
- find-skills: Helps users discover and install agent skills when they ask questions like "how do I do X", "find a skill for X", "is there a skill that can...", or express interest in extending capabilities. This skill should be used when the user is looking for functionality that might exist as an installable skill.
- investigate: Systematic debugging with root cause investigation. (gstack)
- office-hours: YC Office Hours — two modes. (gstack)
- review: Pre-landing PR review. (gstack)
- signing-in-to-aws: Gets AWS credentials for CLI/SDK access via `aws login`. Activates when a developer needs to authenticate to AWS for local development, when an AWS operation fails due to missing or expired credentials, or when someone asks about setting up AWS access. Triggers: "set up AWS", "configure AWS", "aws login", "get credentials", "authenticate", "session expired", "token expired", "no credentials", "AccessDeniedException" with no configured credentials.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- claude-in-chrome: Automates your Chrome browser to interact with web pages - clicking elements, filling forms, capturing screenshots, reading console logs, and navigating sites. Opens pages in new tabs within your existing Chrome session. Requires site-level permissions before executing (configured in the extension). - When the user wants to interact with web pages, automate browser tasks, capture screenshots, read console logs, or perform any browser-based actions. Always invoke BEFORE attempting to use any mcp__claude-in-chrome__* tools.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

aiTitle: Deploy Calibre Web Automated on redu

content.text: I'll start by reading redu.md.

content.content:
1	---
2	redu_schema: 2
3	repo: https://github.com/crocodilestick/Calibre-Web-Automated
4	plan:
5	  tool: deploy_compose
6	  image: crocodilestick/calibre-web-automated:v4.0.6
7	  port: 8083
8	  vm: m1.medium
9	  flavor_id: "3"
10	  database: none. Calibre's library format IS SQLite; do not provision a managed database
11	  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0278
12	bootstrap:
13	  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
14	  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
15	  source: calibre-web-automated
16	quirks:
17	  - "⛔⛔ THE ADMINISTRATOR ALREADY EXISTS AND ITS PASSWORD IS PUBLISHED IN THE README. THIS IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS. Nobody signs up to become admin here: cps/ub.py:1236-1242 creates the account on first boot, whenever /config/app.db is absent, and cps/ub.py:1176-1185 gives it the name admin, every admin role, and the literal at cps/constants.py:132, which README.md:433-434 reprints for everyone. THERE IS NO WAY TO SET IT AT DEPLOY TIME, and the proof is the line next to it: cps/constants.py:132 is a bare literal, while DEFAULT_PORT immediately below at :133-141 IS overridable by an environment variable. The author wired an override for the port and not for the password, and create_admin_user reads the constant directly. So the window opens the instant the container answers on a public hostname, and the ONLY thing that closes it is you changing that password. Rotate it as the immediately-next action after deploy_compose returns, before you hand the URL to anyone, using the script in the body of this file. Do not hand over a URL you have not rotated."
18	  - "ROTATE THROUGH THE SETTINGS DATABASE, NOT THROUGH THE LOGIN FORM, and the reason is specific. The form is CSRF-protected (cps/__init__.py:36,101,118) and rate limited to 3 attempts per MINUTE and 40 per DAY keyed on the submitted username (cps/web.py:2216-2218), so a scripted login that fumbles once locks you out of the very account you are trying to secure, for a minute, and burns a daily budget you cannot reset. Writing the new hash straight into /config/app.db needs no HTTP, no CSRF token and no rate-limit budget, and it works while redu's proxy is still answering 502. AFTERWARDS RESTART THE CONTAINER: the app holds app.db open through a long-lived SQLAlchemy session, so do not assume it re-reads the row."
19	  - "⚠️ THE PASSWORD POLICY WANTS A SYMBOL, WHICH INVERTS THE USUAL HABIT. cps/config_sql.py:168-174 defaults to config_password_policy on, min length 8, plus a digit, plus a lowercase, plus an uppercase, plus a NON-ALPHANUMERIC character, and cps/helper.py:796-813 rejects anything else with \"Password doesn't comply with password validation rules\". The usual advice in this library is to generate alphanumeric-only passwords so there is nothing to escape; here that produces a password the user can never change from the UI afterwards. Generate one that satisfies the policy, and keep the symbol out of shell interpolation by generating it INSIDE the container, as the script does."
20	  - "⛔ PIN v4.0.6. THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE SAYS :latest AND THE REGISTRY IS FULL OF NIGHTLIES. docker-compose.yml:3 ships image: crocodilestick/calibre-web-automated:latest. On Docker Hub the newest RELEASE tag is v4.0.6, pushed 2026-02-04 alongside the GitHub release, while the dev and dev-NNN tags were being pushed as recently as 2026-08-07. Those are development builds, not releases, and a habit-written :latest or a curious :dev is a redeploy that silently crosses six months of unreleased changes on a library you cannot easily roll back. Pin the version."
21	  - "⛔ THERE IS NO DATABASE TO WIRE AND YOU MUST NOT PROVISION ONE. This is the opposite of every other entry in this library, so read it twice. Calibre's library format IS metadata.db, a SQLite file that the bundled calibredb binaries open directly, and the settings store is app.db (cps/constants.py:47), also SQLite. Nothing in the tree speaks Postgres or MySQL and there is no driver variable to set. Passing database:'managed' to deploy_compose provisions a second VM at GBP 0.0174/hr that the app will never open a connection to, and it does not make anything more durable. Durability here is entirely a question of volumes."
22	  - "⛔ THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE IS A TEMPLATE AND DOCKER WILL HAPPILY OBEY IT LITERALLY. docker-compose.yml:33-42 bind-mounts four PLACEHOLDER paths: /path/to/config/folder, /path/to/the/folder/you/want/to/use/for/book/ingest, /path/to/your/calibre/library and /path/to/your/calibre/plugins/folder. Copy that file as it stands and Docker creates those exact directories on the VM, root-owned and empty, the container comes up looking perfectly healthy, and every book and every setting is written somewhere nobody will ever look for or back up. Replace all four with NAMED VOLUMES before you deploy. The plugins mount is optional; drop it unless the user actually has Calibre plugins."
23	  - "THREE VOLUMES, AND /config IS THE ONE HOLDING THE SECRET. Dockerfile:295-297 declares VOLUME /config, /cwa-book-ingest and /calibre-library. /config holds app.db (every user, every session, every setting) and .key, a Fernet key generated on first boot at cps/config_sql.py:605-625 and used at cps/config_sql.py:459-480 to encrypt the stored SMTP and LDAP passwords. THE SECRET HERE IS A FILE, NOT A VARIABLE: there is no way to supply it at deploy time and no way to recreate it, so the volume is the only thing protecting it. /calibre-library holds metadata.db and every book file. Lose either volume and there is nothing to restore from."
24	  - "⚠️ /cwa-book-ingest IS A DROP BOX THAT DELETES WHAT YOU PUT IN IT. docker-compose.yml:36 says so in its own comment: everything placed there is REMOVED AFTER PROCESSING, once the file has been converted and filed into the library. That is correct behaviour and not a bug, but it means the ingest volume is not storage and not a backup, and it must never point at the same volume as the library. Tell the user plainly that a file dropped there disappears from there on success."
25	  - "⛔ DISK IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT, NOT RAM, AND IT IS THE DECISION TO PUT TO THE USER BEFORE YOU DEPLOY. A flavor's disk is fixed at create time: m1.medium is 40 GB TOTAL, shared with Ubuntu, docker and an image that carries a full Calibre install, and what remains is the whole library. m1.large is 80 GB at GBP 0.0486/hr and is ABOVE the no-card trial ceiling of m1.medium. Upstream publishes no per-book figure and neither do we, so ask how many books and in what format BEFORE choosing, and say out loud that growing it later is a volume resize rather than a redeploy. EPUB libraries are small; a comics or PDF library is not."
26	  - "PORT 8083, AND LEAVE CWA_PORT_OVERRIDE UNSET. Dockerfile:294 exposes 8083 and cps/constants.py:133-141 defaults to it. CWA_PORT_OVERRIDE exists but falls back to 8083 on an unparseable value rather than failing, so a typo there gives you a container listening somewhere you did not intend with no error to read. Pass 8083 to deploy_compose and leave the variable out of the compose entirely."
27	  - "LEAVE TRUSTED_PROXY_COUNT AT ITS DEFAULT OF 1. cps/__init__.py:91 wires werkzeug ProxyFix with that count across x_for, x_proto, x_host and x_prefix. redu puts exactly one proxy in front of the VM, so 1 is correct. The compose comments suggest 2 for a Cloudflare Tunnel chain; setting 2 here makes CWA trust an X-Forwarded-For hop that does not exist, which lets a client write its own address into the login rate limiter and the session protection."
28	  - "SET SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true. cps/__init__.py:78 defaults it to False, so out of the box the session cookie is issued without the Secure flag even though redu only ever serves this over TLS. It costs nothing to set and cps/__init__.py:81 already sets WTF_CSRF_SSL_STRICT=False, so it does not break the CSRF check behind a proxy."
29	  - "WHAT AN ANONYMOUS REQUEST REACHES, which is a short list and one surprise. cps/config_sql.py:86-87 defaults config_anonbrowse to 0 and config_public_reg to 0, so there is no signup form and no anonymous browsing: everything in the web UI redirects to /login. Open without any credential: [REDACTED:value] /health (cps/web.py:975-1003, JSON carrying status, uptime and a CWA/<version> string) and the static assets. THE SURPRISE: /opds and the Kobo sync endpoints accept HTTP BASIC auth (cps/opds.py:231-233 via cps/usermanagement.py:141-163), and the shipped default credential is valid there too. So the exposure is two surfaces, not one, and the verification script below deliberately probes /opds rather than the login form."
30	  - "REGISTRATION IS CLOSED AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT AND STAYS CLOSED. config_public_reg defaults to 0 (cps/config_sql.py:87) and there is no first-visitor signup path at all, which is the one thing this app gets right by construction. If the user wants to open it, that is Admin then Edit Basic Configuration then Feature Configuration, and config_register_email (default False) gates it further by requiring a working SMTP setup. Do not turn it on by default."
31	  - "KEEP PUID=1000 AND PGID=1000. The upstream compose ships those and redu's Ubuntu VM has uid and gid 1000, so the named volumes end up owned by the account the container drops to and nothing needs a chown. Set TZ to the user's own zone; it only affects displayed timestamps and the scheduled maintenance tasks."
32	  - "DROP HARDCOVER_TOKEN FROM THE COMPOSE. The upstream file ships that variable with a literal placeholder string in it, which CWA then presents to Hardcover as a metadata provider credential. It is opt-in and it is not needed for anything in this recipe. Delete the line rather than leaving a placeholder in place."
33	  - "NO migrate_command NEEDED. cps/ub.py:1230-1242 creates the schema on a fresh /config and runs migrate_Database plus clean_database on every subsequent boot. The first boot also unpacks and prepares the bundled Calibre binaries, so give the health check generous room: an impatient probe reports a failed deploy on a container that is starting normally."
34	  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.028/hr, roughly GBP 20 a month, inside the no-card free trial) and WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id '3' (m1.medium), NO database argument at all, port 8083. If plan_deploy proposes m1.large because a compose stack is declared, hold m1.medium unless the user has told you the library needs the disk: nothing here is built from source, and the larger floor exists for builds."
35	  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built. Write the trimmed one-service docker-compose.yml locally with named volumes, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Pointing deploy_compose at the GitHub URL would clone a repo full of images and translations to build nothing."
36	  - "LICENCE: GNU GPL version 3, inherited from Calibre-Web, read from the LICENSE file at the repo root. GPL-3.0 has no section 13 network clause, so unlike AGPL it puts NO source-offer obligation on somebody who merely operates the service. The obligation attaches to distributing a modified binary or image. A user running their own instance in their own account has nothing to do."
37	  - "⛔ NEVER WRITE CREDENTIALS INTO THIS FILE. The rotated admin password belongs to the user and this file is committed and read by the next person. Print it once at the end of the deploy, tell them to store it, and record in the log only that the shipped default was rotated and refused, never any value."
38	  - "AFTERWARDS: pass THIS file to get_deployment as redu_md and write the merged redu_md_markdown back. ⚠️ The merge does NOT write new quirks: when this file is richer than redu's template it returns redu_md_merge_mode in_place, refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Anything your run taught you has to be added BY HAND. The two most useful numbers you can add are the idle memory figure and the disk actually left on a 40 GB flavor after the image and an empty library, because upstream publishes neither."
39	  - "DELETING IT DELETES THE BOOKS, and this entry is the exception to the usual reassurance. Most entries here keep a managed database after delete_deployment; this one has no managed database, so the library, the metadata and the settings all live on the app VM's volumes and go with it. There is nothing left billing afterwards and nothing left to recover. Say that plainly before deleting, and offer to copy /calibre-library off the VM first."
40	  - "THIS IS A LIBRARY FOR BOOKS THE USER ALREADY HAS. CWA ingests files the user drops in, converts them, fixes covers and metadata, and serves them over OPDS, Kobo sync and KOReader sync. It has no indexer, no tracker client and no downloader, and nothing in this recipe should add one. Deploying it does not make redu the operator: the instance is the user's, in their own account."
41	---
42	
43	# Self-host Calibre Web Automated on redu
44	
45	Your own ebook library, on your own server, readable from any device: one container, three
46	volumes, a public HTTPS URL, and no database VM to pay for.
47

53	  whatever you put in it.

55	- **No managed database.** Calibre's library format is a SQLite file, so there is nothing to
56	  wire and nothing extra to bill.

72	with the operating system, docker and an image that carries a whole Calibre install inside it.
73	That is comfortable for a few thousand EPUBs and tight for a PDF or comics collection. m1.large
74	doubles it to 80 GB, costs GBP 0.0486/hour, and is above the free trial's ceiling.

84	password that is a literal in the source and republished in the README, and there is no
85	environment variable that lets you set a different one at deploy time. From the moment the
86	container answers on a public hostname until you change that password, the credential that opens
87	your library is public knowledge.

89	So the recipe treats rotation as part of the deploy rather than as advice. The script below writes
90	a fresh password straight into the settings database, restarts the container, and then proves both
91	halves: that the shipped default is refused, and that the new one works. It deliberately does not
92	go through the login form, which is CSRF-protected and rate limited to three attempts a minute.

95

97	safe to run while redu's proxy is still answering 502.

100	#!/usr/bin/env bash
101	# Rotate the shipped Calibre-Web-Automated admin credential and PROVE the rotation took.
102	# Exit 0 = rotated and verified. 1 = failed, deal with it now. 2 = could not run.
103	# 3 = INCONCLUSIVE, could not tell; re-run rather than believing it.
104	set -eu -o pipefail
105	
106	HOST="${1:-}"
107	[ -n "$HOST" ] || { echo "usage: rotate-cwa-admin.sh <app-hostname>" >&2; exit 2; }
108	
109	C="$(sudo docker ps --filter name=calibre --format '{{.Names}}' | head -n 1)"
110	[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "FAIL: no calibre container is running. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }
111	
112	# 1. Wait for the settings database the image creates on its first boot.
113	i=0
114	while [ "$i" -lt 60 ]; do
115	  sudo docker exec "$C" test -f /config/app.db && break
116	  i=$((i + 1)); sleep 5
117	done
118	sudo docker exec "$C" test -f /config/app.db \
119	  || { echo "FAIL: /config/app.db never appeared. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }
120	
121	# 2. Read the shipped default OUT OF THE IMAGE rather than hardcoding it, so this keeps working
122	#    if upstream ever changes it, and so no credential lives in this file.
123	DEFAULTPW="$(sudo docker exec -i "$C" python3 - <<'PY'
124	import re
125	src = open("/app/calibre-web-automated/cps/constants.py").read()
126	m = re.search(r'DEFAULT_PASSWORD\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"', src)
127	print(m.group(1) if m else "")
128	PY
129	)"

131	
132	# 3. Generate the new one INSIDE the container, so it never appears in any process argument list,
133	#    and satisfy the default policy: a digit, both cases and a non-alphanumeric character.
134	NEWPASS="[REDACTED:value] docker exec -i "$C" python3 - <<'PY'
135	import secrets, sqlite3, string
136	from werkzeug.security import generate_password_hash
137	pw = "".join(secrets.choice(string.ascii_letters + string.digits) for _ in range(24)) + "aA1!"
138	db = sqlite3.connect("/config/app.db", timeout=30)
139	n = db.execute("UPDATE user SET password = ? WHERE name = ?",
140	               (generate_password_hash(pw), "admin")).rowcount
141	db.commit(); db.close()
142	if n != 1:
143	    raise SystemExit("expected exactly one admin row, updated %d" % n)
144	print(pw)
145	PY
146	)"
147	[ -n "$NEWPASS" ] || { echo "FAIL: the rotation did not run. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }
148	
149	# 4. The app holds app.db open through a long-lived session, so restart rather than assume.
150	sudo docker restart "$C" >/dev/null
151	
152	# 5. Gate every assertion on proof that we are talking to CWA and not to an error page.
153	#    redu's proxy answers 502 for roughly the first 2.5 minutes of a container start, and an
154	#    error page fails every "did it NOT do X" check by accident.
155	i=0; code=000; body=""
156	while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
157	  code="$(curl -sS -o /tmp/cwa-health -w '%{http_code}' -L "https://$HOST/health" || echo 000)"
158	  body="$(cat /tmp/cwa-health 2>/dev/null || true)"
159	  [ "$code" = "200" ] && break
160	  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "still starting (502 from the proxy), re-checking"
161	  i=$((i + 1)); sleep 15
162	done
163	[ "$code" = "200" ] || {
164	  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /health never returned 200 (last $code). Re-run; do not report a result." >&2
165	  exit 3; }
166	case "$body" in
167	  *"CWA/"*) : ;;
168	  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /health but the body is not CWA's. Something else is on this host." >&2
169	     exit 3 ;;
170	esac
171	rm -f /tmp/cwa-health
172	
173	# 6. BOTH HALVES, and the positive one FIRST. If /opds did not exist, both probes would answer
174	#    the same thing and a negative-only check would print a green pass on a wide-open instance.
175	new_code="$(printf 'user = "admin:%s"\n' "$NEWPASS" \
176	  | curl -sS -K - -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/opds")"
177	old_code="$(printf 'user = "admin:%s"\n' "$DEFAULTPW" \
178	  | curl -sS -K - -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/opds")"
179	
180	[ "$new_code" = "200" ] || {
181	  echo "FAIL: the new credential does not authenticate ($new_code), so the next check proves nothing." >&2
182	  exit 1; }
183	[ "$old_code" = "401" ] || {
184	  echo "FAIL: the SHIPPED DEFAULT still authenticates ($old_code). Delete this deployment now." >&2
185	  exit 1; }
186	
187	echo "OK: shipped default refused with 401, rotated credential accepted with 200."
188	echo "Admin username: admin"
189	echo "Admin password: [REDACTED:value]"
190	echo "Hand this to the user now. Do not write it into redu.md or into any log."

  - "⚠️ THE PASSWORD POLICY WANTS A SYMBOL, WHICH INVERTS THE USUAL HABIT. cps/config_sql.py:168-174 defaults to config_password_policy on, min length 8, plus a digit, plus a lowercase, plus an uppercase, plus a NON-ALPHANUMERIC character, and cps/helper.py:796-813 rejects anything else with \"Password doesn't comply with password validation rules\".   - "⛔ THERE IS NO DATABASE TO WIRE AND YOU MUST NOT PROVISION ONE. This is the opposite of every other entry in this library, so read it twice.   - "⛔ THE UPSTREAM COMPOSE IS A TEMPLATE AND DOCKER WILL HAPPILY OBEY IT LITERALLY. docker-compose.yml:33-42 bind-mounts four PLACEHOLDER paths: /path/to/config/folder, /path/to/the/folder/you/want/to/use/for/book/ingest, /path/to/your/calibre/library and /path/to/your/calibre/plugins/folder. Tell the user plainly that a file dropped there disappears from there on success."
  - "⛔ DISK IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT, NOT RAM, AND IT IS THE DECISION TO PUT TO THE USER BEFORE YOU DEPLOY. EPUB libraries are small; a comics or PDF library is not."
  - "PORT 8083, AND LEAVE CWA_PORT_OVERRIDE UNSET. Dockerfile:294 exposes 8083 and cps/constants.py:133-141 defaults to it.   - "SET SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true. cps/__init__.py:78 defaults it to False, so out of the box the session cookie is issued without the Secure flag even though redu only ever serves this over TLS.   - "REGISTRATION IS CLOSED AFTER THE FIRST ACCOUNT AND STAYS CLOSED. config_public_reg defaults to 0 (cps/config_sql.py:87) and there is no first-visitor signup path at all, which is the one thing this app gets right by construction. The upstream compose ships those and redu's Ubuntu VM has uid and gid 1000, so the named volumes end up owned by the account the container drops to and nothing needs a chown.   - "DROP HARDCOVER_TOKEN FROM THE COMPOSE. The upstream file ships that variable with a literal placeholder string in it, which CWA then presents to Hardcover as a metadata provider credential. # Self-host Calibre Web Automated on redu

Your own ebook library, on your own server, readable from any device: one container, three
volumes, a public HTTPS URL, and no database VM to pay for.

## What this deploys

- **Calibre Web Automated** from the official image, pinned to a release, on one m1.medium VM,
  port 8083.
- **Three volumes**: your library, the settings database, and a drop folder that auto-ingests
  whatever you put in it.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.
- **No managed database.** Calibre's library format is a SQLite file, so there is nothing to
  wire and nothing extra to bill.

About GBP 0.028/hour, roughly GBP 20 a month. Inside the no-card free trial.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Calibre Web Automated on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## One decision to make before you deploy: how big is the library?

Disk comes with the flavor and is fixed at create time. m1.medium gives you 40 GB in total, shared
with the operating system, docker and an image that carries a whole Calibre install inside it.
That is comfortable for a few thousand EPUBs and tight for a PDF or comics collection. m1.large
doubles it to 80 GB, costs GBP 0.0486/hour, and is above the free trial's ceiling.

Growing it afterwards is a volume resize, not a redeploy, so it is worth answering the question
now rather than discovering it at 90% full.

## The one that actually breaks it

**The administrator already exists, and its password is printed in the project's own README.**

Nobody signs up to claim this instance. The image creates an `admin` account on first boot with a
password that is a literal in the source and republished in the README, and there is no
environment variable that lets you set a different one at deploy time. From the moment the
container answers on a public hostname until you change that password, the credential that opens
your library is public knowledge.

So the recipe treats rotation as part of the deploy rather than as advice. The script below writes
a fresh password straight into the settings database, restarts the container, and then proves both
halves: that the shipped default is refused, and that the new one works. It deliberately does not
go through the login form, which is CSRF-protected and rate limited to three attempts a minute.

## Close the window

Run this on the app VM, over SSH, as the immediately-next action after the deploy returns. It is
safe to run while redu's proxy is still answering 502.

```bash

# Rotate the shipped Calibre-Web-Automated admin credential and PROVE the rotation took.
# Exit 0 = rotated and verified. 1 = failed, deal with it now. 2 = could not run.
# 3 = INCONCLUSIVE, could not tell; re-run rather than believing it.
set -eu -o pipefail

HOST="${1:-}"
[ -n "$HOST" ] || { echo "usage: rotate-cwa-admin.sh <app-hostname>" >&2; exit 2; }

C="$(sudo docker ps --filter name=calibre --format '{{.Names}}' | head -n 1)"
[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "FAIL: no calibre container is running. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }

# 1. Wait for the settings database the image creates on its first boot.
i=0
while [ "$i" -lt 60 ]; do
  sudo docker exec "$C" test -f /config/app.db && break
  i=$((i + 1)); sleep 5
done
sudo docker exec "$C" test -f /config/app.db \
  || { echo "FAIL: /config/app.db never appeared. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }

# 2. Read the shipped default OUT OF THE IMAGE rather than hardcoding it, so this keeps working
#    if upstream ever changes it, and so no credential lives in this file.
DEFAULTPW="$(sudo docker exec -i "$C" python3 - <<'PY'
import re
src = open("/app/calibre-web-automated/cps/constants.py").read()
m = re.search(r'DEFAULT_PASSWORD\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"', src)
print(m.group(1) if m else "")
PY
)"
[ -n "$DEFAULTPW" ] || { echo "FAIL: could not read the shipped default out of the image." >&2; exit 2; }

# 3. Generate the new one INSIDE the container, so it never appears in any process argument list,
#    and satisfy the default policy: a digit, both cases and a non-alphanumeric character.
NEWPASS="[REDACTED:value] docker exec -i "$C" python3 - <<'PY'

n = db.execute("UPDATE user SET password = ? WHERE name = ?",
               (generate_password_hash(pw), "admin")).rowcount
db.commit(); db.close()
if n != 1:
    raise SystemExit("expected exactly one admin row, updated %d" % n)
print(pw)
PY
)"
[ -n "$NEWPASS" ] || { echo "FAIL: the rotation did not run. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }

# 4. The app holds app.db open through a long-lived session, so restart rather than assume.
sudo docker restart "$C" >/dev/null

# 5. Gate every assertion on proof that we are talking to CWA and not to an error page.
#    redu's proxy answers 502 for roughly the first 2.5 minutes of a container start, and an
#    error page fails every "did it NOT do X" check by accident.
i=0; code=000; body=""
while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
  code="$(curl -sS -o /tmp/cwa-health -w '%{http_code}' -L "https://$HOST/health" || echo 000)"
  body="$(cat /tmp/cwa-health 2>/dev/null || true)"
  [ "$code" = "200" ] && break
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "still starting (502 from the proxy), re-checking"
  i=$((i + 1)); sleep 15
done
[ "$code" = "200" ] || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /health never returned 200 (last $code). Re-run; do not report a result." >&2
  exit 3; }
case "$body" in
  *"CWA/"*) : ;;
  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /health but the body is not CWA's. Something else is on this host." >&2
     exit 3 ;;
esac
rm -f /tmp/cwa-health

# 6. BOTH HALVES, and the positive one FIRST. If /opds did not exist, both probes would answer
#    the same thing and a negative-only check would print a green pass on a wide-open instance.
new_code="$(printf 'user = "admin:%s"\n' "$NEWPASS" \
  | curl -sS -K - -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/opds")"
old_code="$(printf 'user = "admin:%s"\n' "$DEFAULTPW" \
  | curl -sS -K - -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/opds")"

[ "$new_code" = "200" ] || {
  echo "FAIL: the new credential does not authenticate ($new_code), so the next check proves nothing." >&2
  exit 1; }
[ "$old_code" = "401" ] || {
  echo "FAIL: the SHIPPED DEFAULT still authenticates ($old_code). Delete this deployment now." >&2
  exit 1; }

echo "OK: shipped default refused with 401, rotated credential accepted with 200."
echo "Admin username: admin"
echo "Admin password: [REDACTED:value]"
echo "Hand this to the user now. Do not write it into redu.md or into any log."
```

## What you get once it is up

- A web reader and library UI, with covers, series, shelves and full-text search.
- An **OPDS** catalogue at `/opds` that Moon+ Reader, KyBook, Panels and most other readers
  speak natively.
- **Kobo sync** and **KOReader** progress sync, so a device syncs against your server rather than
  a vendor's.
- An **ingest folder**: drop a file in, and it is converted, filed and given proper metadata.
  Note that the file is removed from the drop folder once it has been filed.

## Licence, since it is a fair question

GPL-3.0, inherited from Calibre-Web. Unlike AGPL there is no network clause, so running it as a
service for yourself creates no obligation to publish anything. The obligation only attaches if
you distribute a modified build.

Here's the plan. redu's planner proposed **m1.large** because it sees a compose stack, but that's a *build* floor — nothing is built here, it's one pre-built image. The recipe says hold m1.medium unless the library needs the disk, so that's the real decision:

| | m1.medium (recipe default) | m1.large |
|---|---|---|
| Cost | **GBP 0.0278/hr ≈ £20/mo** | GBP 0.0486/hr ≈ £35/mo |
| Disk | 40 GB total, shared with Ubuntu + Docker + a full Calibre install | 80 GB |
| Free trial | inside the no-card ceiling | **above** it |

One VM, port 8083, **no database** (Calibre's library format *is* SQLite — a managed DB would bill and never be connected to), three named volumes (`/config`, `/calibre-library`, `/cwa-book-ingest`), one public HTTPS URL. Disk is fixed at create time; growing later is a volume resize, not a redeploy.

One thing you should know before saying go: **the admin account already exists and its password is printed in the project's own README.** There's no way to set it at deploy time. I'll rotate it through the settings database as the immediately-next action after the deploy returns, restart the container, and prove both halves (old refused, new accepted) before I hand you the URL.

services:
  calibre-web-automated:
    image: crocodilestick/calibre-web-automated:v4.0.6
    container_name: calibre-web-automated
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports:
      - "8083:8083"
    environment:
      - PUID=1000
      - PGID=1000
      - TZ=Etc/UTC
      # redu terminates TLS in front of the VM; issue the session cookie with Secure.
      - SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=true
    volumes:
      # Settings database (app.db) and the Fernet .key. Losing this loses every user and setting.
      - cwa-config:/config
      # Drop box: files placed here are ingested, filed into the library, then REMOVED from here.
      - cwa-book-ingest:/cwa-book-ingest
      # The library itself: metadata.db and every book file.
      - cwa-library:/calibre-library

volumes:
  cwa-config:
  cwa-book-ingest:
  cwa-library:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Rotate the shipped Calibre-Web-Automated admin credential and PROVE the rotation took.
# Exit 0 = rotated and verified. 1 = failed, deal with it now. 2 = could not run.
# 3 = INCONCLUSIVE, could not tell; re-run rather than believing it.
set -eu -o pipefail

HOST="${1:-}"
[ -n "$HOST" ] || { echo "usage: rotate-cwa-admin.sh <app-hostname>" >&2; exit 2; }

C="$(sudo docker ps --filter name=calibre --format '{{.Names}}' | head -n 1)"
[ -n "$C" ] || { echo "FAIL: no calibre container is running. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }

# 1. Wait for the settings database the image creates on its first boot.
i=0
while [ "$i" -lt 60 ]; do
  sudo docker exec "$C" test -f /config/app.db && break
  i=$((i + 1)); sleep 5
done
sudo docker exec "$C" test -f /config/app.db \
  || { echo "FAIL: /config/app.db never appeared. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }

# 2. Read the shipped default OUT OF THE IMAGE rather than hardcoding it, so this keeps working
#    if upstream ever changes it, and so no credential lives in this file.
DEFAULTPW="$(sudo docker exec -i "$C" python3 - <<'PY'
import re
src = open("/app/calibre-web-automated/cps/constants.py").read()
m = re.search(r'DEFAULT_PASSWORD\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"', src)
print(m.group(1) if m else "")
PY
)"
[ -n "$DEFAULTPW" ] || { echo "FAIL: could not read the shipped default out of the image." >&2; exit 2; }

# 3. Generate the new one INSIDE the container, so it never appears in any process argument list,
#    and satisfy the default policy: a digit, both cases and a non-alphanumeric character.
NEWPASS="[REDACTED:value] docker exec -i "$C" python3 - <<'PY'
import secrets, sqlite3, string
from werkzeug.security import generate_password_hash
pw = "".join(secrets.choice(string.ascii_letters + string.digits) for _ in range(24)) + "aA1!"
db = sqlite3.connect("/config/app.db", timeout=30)
n = db.execute("UPDATE user SET password = ? WHERE name = ?",
               (generate_password_hash(pw), "admin")).rowcount
db.commit(); db.close()
if n != 1:
    raise SystemExit("expected exactly one admin row, updated %d" % n)
print(pw)
PY
)"
[ -n "$NEWPASS" ] || { echo "FAIL: the rotation did not run. Do not leave this instance up." >&2; exit 2; }

# 4. The app holds app.db open through a long-lived session, so restart rather than assume.
sudo docker restart "$C" >/dev/null

# 5. Gate every assertion on proof that we are talking to CWA and not to an error page.
#    redu's proxy answers 502 for roughly the first 2.5 minutes of a container start, and an
#    error page fails every "did it NOT do X" check by accident.
i=0; code=000; body=""
while [ "$i" -lt 40 ]; do
  code="$(curl -sS -o /tmp/cwa-health -w '%{http_code}' -L "https://$HOST/health" || echo 000)"
  body="$(cat /tmp/cwa-health 2>/dev/null || true)"
  [ "$code" = "200" ] && break
  [ "$code" = "502" ] && echo "still starting (502 from the proxy), re-checking"
  i=$((i + 1)); sleep 15
done
[ "$code" = "200" ] || {
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: /health never returned 200 (last $code). Re-run; do not report a result." >&2
  exit 3; }
case "$body" in
  *"CWA/"*) : ;;
  *) echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 200 from /health but the body is not CWA's. Something else is on this host." >&2
     exit 3 ;;
esac
rm -f /tmp/cwa-health

# 6. BOTH HALVES, and the positive one FIRST. If /opds did not exist, both probes would answer
#    the same thing and a negative-only check would print a green pass on a wide-open instance.
new_code="$(printf 'user = "admin:%s"\n' "$NEWPASS" \
  | curl -sS -K - -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/opds")"
old_code="$(printf 'user = "admin:%s"\n' "$DEFAULTPW" \
  | curl -sS -K - -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}' "https://$HOST/opds")"

[ "$new_code" = "200" ] || {
  echo "FAIL: the new credential does not authenticate ($new_code), so the next check proves nothing." >&2
  exit 1; }
[ "$old_code" = "401" ] || {
  echo "FAIL: the SHIPPED DEFAULT still authenticates ($old_code). Delete this deployment now." >&2
  exit 1; }

echo "OK: shipped default refused with 401, rotated credential accepted with 200."
echo "Admin username: admin"
echo "Admin password: [REDACTED:value]"
echo "Hand this to the user now. Do not write it into redu.md or into any log."

content.text:
Deployed and secured.

## Your library

**https://calibre-web-automated-he6pn87l.redu.cloud**

```
username: admin
password: «REDACTED:assigned:28d715d3»
```

**Store that now** — it exists nowhere else. I deliberately did not write it into `redu.md`, the plan file, or any log, and I verified with a grep that it appears in no file in the directory.

**The window is closed.** The shipped default (the one printed in the project's README) is refused with `401` on `/opds`; your new password is accepted with `200`. Both halves were proved, in that order, against the live public URL — the rotation went through `/config/app.db` rather than the CSRF-protected, rate-limited login form, and the container was restarted so the app re-read the row.

Anonymous checks from outside: `/` redirects to `/login`, `/opds` without credentials returns `401`, `/health` returns `{"status":"ok",...,"version":"CWA/v4.0.6"}`. There is no signup form, and registration stays closed unless you open it.

## What's running

One m1.medium VM, **GBP 0.0278/hr (~£20.29/mo)**, billed hourly. No database — Calibre's library format *is* SQLite, so there was nothing to provision. Three named volumes: `cwa-config` (settings + the Fernet key), `cwa-library` (books + metadata), `cwa-book-ingest` (drop folder). Image pinned to `v4.0.6`, not `:latest`.

Two things to know as the operator:
- **The ingest folder deletes what you put in it.** That's correct behaviour — a file dropped in `/cwa-book-ingest` is converted, filed into the library, and removed from the drop folder. It is not storage and not a backup.
- **Deleting this deployment deletes the books.** There's no managed database holding anything back; the library lives on this VM's volumes. Ask me to copy `/calibre-library` off first if that day comes.

## Disk

4.7 GB of 38 GB usable is consumed by Ubuntu, Docker and the 2.44 GB image, leaving **~34 GB for books**. Idle memory is 146 MiB, so RAM is nowhere near the constraint — disk is. Growing it later is a volume resize, not a redeploy.

## One thing worth flagging

The deploy took **~2h55m** end to end, but the container was healthy in **8 minutes** — the compose runner logged `result status=ready healthy=1` at 17:28:27 UTC. The remaining ~2h45m was redu's control plane finishing the floating-IP and proxy step, with three other deploys provisioning on the same tenant. Nothing was wrong and nothing needed fixing, but during that gap the hostname fails TLS and SSH is unavailable, so it looks identical to a broken deploy. I've recorded that in `redu.md` as a quirk with the specific tell (check the tail of `build_log` for the compose result line) so the next run doesn't redeploy or resize in a panic.

Files written: `docker-compose.yml` (trimmed, three named volumes, no placeholder bind mounts, no `HARDCOVER_TOKEN`), `redu-deploy-plan.md` (real deployed values), and `redu.md` — hand-edited rather than server-merged, so your accumulated quirks stayed byte-for-byte intact while I added the deploy log entry and the three new quirks this run taught, including the two numbers the file asked a first real run to measure.
